title: Availability maths and failure domains
summary: Serial parts multiply, redundant parts add nines only when they fail independently. Failure domains, blast radius, cells, shuffle sharding, and the N+1 headroom you need to lose a zone.

steps.title: Serial parts multiply, redundant parts add nines
body: A request that needs **every** part in a chain succeeds only if all of them work. Availabilities multiply:
```text
load balancer 99.99%  ->  app 99.9%  ->  database 99.95%
A = 0.9999 x 0.999 x 0.9995 = 0.9984   (99.84%: worse than the weakest part)
Every hard dependency you add makes the whole thing **less** available. Ten parts at 99.9% give 99.0%.
Redundant copies work the other way. The tier is down only if **all** copies are down at once:
```text
one app server     99%     -> down 1 in 100
two, independent   1 - (1 - 0.99)^2 = 99.99%
three, independent 1 - (1 - 0.99)^3 = 99.9999%
So you design by putting redundancy into every tier of the serial chain, then multiplying the tiers.
The catch is the word **independent**. That is the rest of this lesson.

steps.prompt: Three tiers in a row: two at 99.9% and one at 99.95%. What does this print?
steps.explain: 0.999 x 0.999 = 0.998001; times 0.9995 is 0.99750. Three good parts in series already lose a quarter of a percent: about 108 minutes a month.

steps.title: Failure domains and blast radius
body: Redundancy only counts when the copies do not share a cause of failure. A **failure domain** is a set of
things that fail together:
| Failure domain | Typical causes | Copies must be in different... |
| process, instance | crash, bad deploy on one host, full disk | instances |
| host, rack | power supply, top-of-rack switch | hosts (anti-affinity) |
| availability zone (AZ) | power, cooling, networking of one data centre group | zones |
| region | regional control plane, a bad regional deploy, a large disaster | regions |
| global | one config push, one DNS change, one certificate, one deploy pipeline | ... time: roll out slowly |
- **Failure domain**: a group of components that a single fault takes down together.
- **Blast radius**: how many users or requests one fault can hurt.
- **Cell**: a complete, independent copy of the service that serves a slice of users. A bad deploy or a poison request hurts one cell, not everyone.
- **Shuffle sharding**: each customer gets a random small set of workers (say 2 of 8). Two customers rarely share the same set (1 in 28 here), so one noisy customer cannot take down everyone.
The most common "redundant but not really" failure is the **global** row: two regions that take the same bad
config at the same minute fail together. Roll changes out one domain at a time.

steps.prompt: Is this real redundancy, or do the copies share fate?
items: Two app instances in different availability zones
Two app instances on the same physical host
A database primary and a synchronous standby in different zones
Two regions that read their config from one global flag service with no local copy
Two regions deployed by the same pipeline in the same minute
Three cache nodes spread across three zones
steps.explain: Count copies only across the failure domain you are protecting against. A shared host, a shared config source or a simultaneous deploy is one failure domain, however many boxes you draw.

steps.prompt: A multi-tenant API runs 8 workers. One tenant sends requests that crash any worker that handles them. Why does giving each tenant a **shuffle shard** of 2 random workers help?
options: The bad tenant can crash only its own 2 workers; almost every other tenant has at least one worker outside that pair
It stops the crash from happening
It makes the bad tenant's requests faster
It doubles the capacity of every tenant
explain: With 8 workers there are 28 possible pairs, so only about 1 tenant in 28 shares both of the bad tenant's workers.
Everyone else keeps a healthy worker and, with retries to the other worker in their shard, sees little impact.
Without sharding, the poison requests would spread to all 8 workers and take everyone down.

steps.title: N+1: headroom to lose a zone
body: Spreading across zones only helps if the zones that are left can carry the **whole** peak. Lose one of
`n` zones and each survivor takes `n / (n - 1)` times its load:
```text
zones   load per zone before   after losing one   so run below
"Run below" is the ceiling just to *fit*. You also want a sane utilisation **after** the loss (queueing
explodes near 100%, module 2), so multiply by your target: at a 70% target with 3 zones, run below about 47%
before the loss. That is why three zones are popular: the spare capacity is a third, not half.
Autoscaling does not replace headroom. New instances take minutes to boot, and when a whole zone fails,
everyone in that region asks for capacity at the same moment. Step through the numbers:

code: Console.WriteLine($"{zones} zones: fit below {Math.Round(fit * 100)}%, keep {Math.Round(target * 100)}% after a loss below {Math.Round(safe * 100)}%");

steps.prompt: Three zones, each running at 60% CPU at peak. One zone fails and its traffic spreads evenly over the other two. What does this print?
steps.explain: The same work now runs on two thirds of the machines: 60% x 3 / 2 = 90%. It fits, but at 90% the queues are long, so p99 climbs sharply until you add capacity.

prompt: **Dashboard after a zone failure.** Checkout runs in 3 zones with autoscaling on. Zone b lost power at 14:02.
Which change would have prevented what you see?
code: time    zones up  instances  CPU (avg)  p99      5xx
options: Run enough instances that 2 zones carry the peak at a sane utilisation (about 45 instances here), instead of relying on the autoscaler
Faster health checks on the load balancer
Move all instances into the healthiest zone
explain: At 72% across 3 zones, the 2 survivors needed 108% of their capacity: queues grew and requests failed until
new instances booted 7 minutes later. Headroom of a third (N+1 per zone) absorbs the loss at once. The
autoscaler then restores the spare capacity, rather than being on the critical path. Putting everything in one

steps.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Components that one fault takes down together
How much of the user base one fault can hurt
An independent full copy of the service for a slice of users
Each customer gets a random small subset of workers
Enough capacity that losing any one zone still fits the peak

steps.title: Availability of a design
prompt: Write three methods:
- `double Serial(params double[] parts)`: the availability of parts that are **all** needed (multiply them).
`Serial()` with no parts is `1`.
- `double Parallel(double a, int n)`: the availability of `n` independent copies of a part with
availability `a`, where one working copy is enough: `1 - (1 - a)^n`. `n` below 1 throws `ArgumentException`.
- `double DowntimeMinutes(double availability)`: expected minutes down in a 30-day month (43,200 minutes).
`Serial(Parallel(0.99, 2), 0.9995)` is about `0.9994`: two app servers at 99% in front of a 99.95% database.
solution: foreach (var p in parts) a *= p;
if (n < 1) throw new ArgumentException("need at least one copy", nameof(n));
hints: Start `Serial` at `1.0` and multiply each part in.
`Parallel` is `1 - Math.Pow(1 - a, n)`; check `n` first.
template: Dojo.Eq("no parts: nothing can fail", 1.0, Serial());
Dojo.Eq("one copy is just the part", 0.95, Math.Round(Parallel(0.95, 1), 6));
Dojo.Eq("redundant app tier in front of a database", 0.9994, Math.Round(Serial(Parallel(0.99, 2), 0.9995), 4));
Dojo.Eq("99.9% is 43.2 minutes a month", 43.2, Math.Round(DowntimeMinutes(0.999), 1));
Dojo.Eq("downtime of the three-tier chain", 107.9, Math.Round(DowntimeMinutes(Serial(0.999, 0.999, 0.9995)), 1));
Dojo.Throws<ArgumentException>("zero copies is an error", () => Parallel(0.99, 0));

steps.title: Size the pool to lose a zone
prompt: Write two methods:
- `double MaxUtilToSurvive(int zones)`: the highest utilisation you can run at so that losing one zone still
fits: `(zones - 1) / zones`. Fewer than 2 zones throws `ArgumentException` (one zone cannot survive its own loss).
- `int InstancesNeeded(double peakQps, double qpsPerInstance, int zones)`: instances in total, spread evenly,
so that after losing **one** zone the others still serve `peakQps` with each instance at most
`qpsPerInstance` (already your target, for example the QPS one instance handles at 70% CPU). Work out the
instances per zone (rounded **up**), then multiply by `zones`. Fewer than 2 zones throws `ArgumentException`.
`InstancesNeeded(20000, 500, 3)` is `60`: 40 instances must survive, that is 20 in each of the 2 zones left,
so 20 per zone in all 3.
starter: int InstancesNeeded(double peakQps, double qpsPerInstance, int zones)
solution: if (zones < 2) throw new ArgumentException("one zone cannot survive its own loss", nameof(zones));
int InstancesNeeded(double peakQps, double qpsPerInstance, int zones)
if (zones < 2) throw new ArgumentException("one zone cannot survive its own loss", nameof(zones));
hints: After the loss, `zones - 1` zones must hold `peakQps / qpsPerInstance` instances between them.
template: Dojo.Eq("the same on 2 zones costs more", 80, InstancesNeeded(20_000, 500, 2));
Dojo.Throws<ArgumentException>("one zone cannot survive its own loss", () => InstancesNeeded(1_000, 100, 1));

steps.title: Build it: lose a zone
prompt: In the **System design board**, a busy service runs in one zone with no load balancer health checks and no
database standby. The load test kills availability zone a at peak. Spread the app servers across three
zones with N+1 headroom, turn on health checks, give the database a standby in another zone (and the cache a
replica), then meet the availability, p99 and budget goals the board shows.
steps.explain: Watch the dashboard at the moment the zone dies: the error spike is the health-check detection time and the database failover; the latency bump is the survivors' utilisation. Headroom you paid for in advance is what keeps p99 flat.
